title: Relations Between the Uniform MQ Assumption and Other Multivariate Assumptions
authors: Zijun Zhuang, Yingjie Zhang, and Jintai Ding
abstract:
The uniform multivariate quadratic (UMQ) assumption states that it is hard to find a zero of a uniformly generated MQ function. It is the average-case hardness assumption about the MQ problem. In this paper, we investigate the relations among the UMQ assumption, the MQ one-wayness (MQOW) assumption, and the MQ second-preimage resistance (MQSPR) assumption.

We show that UMQ and MQSPR tightly imply each other, and MQOW tightly implies UMQ. Then, we show that UMQ implies MQOW when $m\leq n+O(\log\lambda)$, where $n$ is the number of variables, $m$ is the number of MQ equations, and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. In particular, when $m\leq n+O(1)$, this implication is tight.

As a corollary, we show that  MQSPR implies MQOW under the same condition $m\leq n+O(\log\lambda)$, which is weaker than the compression condition $n=m+\omega(\log\lambda)$ required for the implication from SPR to OW for general function families. In particular, our result covers the square case $m=n$ as well as mildly overdetermined MQ systems satisfying $m=n+O(\log\lambda)$.

1      Introduction
The multivariate quadratic (MQ) problem asks one to ﬁnd a zero of an MQ
function over a ﬁnite ﬁeld. It is well-studied in multivariate cryptography [15]:
on the one hand, it is NP-hard in the worst case [25]; on the other hand, it is
widely believed to be hard on average for an extensive range of parameters, since
research on algorithms for solving MQ systems [3, 8, 9, 18–21, 23, 33, 38] indicates
that the best known algorithms have exponential complexity when m = Θ(n),
where n is the number of variables and m is the number of MQ equations.
2      Zijun Zhuang, Yingjie Zhang, and Jintai Ding

    The MQ problem has many applications in cryptography, including pseudo-
random generators [5,32], encryption schemes [16,27,37], signature schemes [4,6,
12,29], commitment schemes [10], oblivious transfer protocols [31], zero-knowledge
protocols [13,36], hash functions [7,17,39], and proof-of-work for blockchain [14].
Since there are many average-case assumptions related to the security of these
constructions, we introduce some of them and investigate their relations in this
paper.
    MQ One-Wayness (MQOW) Assumption. One-way functions are fun-
damental cryptographic primitives [26,28,35]. The MQ one-wayness (MQOW) [12]
assumption states that the MQ function family is one-way: given an MQ func-
tion and an output generated from an unknown input, it is computationally
hard to ﬁnd a preimage. Thus, when we consider the MQOW experiment, it is
guaranteed that a preimage exists.
    MQOW has been used to construct a variety of cryptographic primitives.
Berbain et al. [5] constructed the QUAD pseudorandom generator, whose se-
curity is reduced to MQOW. Sakumoto et al. [36] constructed public-key iden-
tiﬁcation schemes based on MQOW. Building on their identiﬁcation protocol,
Chen et al. [12] proposed MQDSS, the ﬁrst provably secure multivariate signa-
ture scheme. Two works in 2024 [4, 22] used the MPC-in-the-Head paradigms to
construct signature schemes based on MQOW.
    MQ Second-Preimage Resistance (MQSPR) Assumption. Second-
preimage resistance (SPR) is a standard security property of cryptographic hash
functions [34]. Since MQ functions can be used to construct hash functions [1,
7, 17], we consider the MQ second-preimage resistance (MQSPR) assumption.
The MQSPR assumption states that the MQ function family is second-preimage
resistant [36, 40]: given an MQ function and a preimage, it is computationally
hard to ﬁnd another preimage with the same image. From the perspective of
solving an MQ system, MQSPR says that the given solution does not reveal
enough information on other solutions.
    MQSPR has been used to establish the security of some cryptosystems. Saku-
moto et al. [36] used MQSPR to prove that the parallel repetition of their MQ-
based identiﬁcation protocol is secure against impersonation under active at-
tacks. Zhuang et al. [40] used MQSPR and other properties of MQ functions to
obtain a provably secure MQ-based one-time signature scheme in the standard
model.
    Uniform MQ (UMQ) Assumption. The uniform MQ (UMQ) assumption
is the average-case hardness assumption about the MQ problem [13], which
states that it is computationally hard to ﬁnd a zero of an MQ function sampled
uniformly at random. UMQ is diﬀerent from MQOW, since a randomly generated
MQ function may not have a zero.
    UMQ has attracted growing attention in cryptography due to its applications
in constructing non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) arguments and ZAPs
(two-message public-coin witness-indistinguishable proofs). Dao et al. (CRYPTO
2024) constructed NIZK arguments based on UMQ and other assumptions [13].
In their construction, UMQ is used to obtain correlation-intractable hash func-

    Their Diﬀerences and Relations. Although UMQ, MQOW, and MQSPR
are all natural average-case assumptions related to the MQ problem, they in-
volve diﬀerent instance distributions and computational tasks. In UMQ, the MQ
system is sampled uniformly at random and may have no solution. In MQOW,
the system is generated together with an unknown solution. In MQSPR, the as-
sociated MQ system has a known solution (i.e., the given preimage), but the goal
is to ﬁnd another one. These diﬀerences make the reduction relations among the
three assumptions nontrivial. Although it has been shown that MQOW implies
MQSPR [40], clarifying the role of UMQ among these multivariate assumptions
is important both for the theory of multivariate cryptography and for the con-
struction of provably secure cryptographic schemes based on the MQ problem.

5    Conclusion
This paper clariﬁes the relations among UMQ, MQOW, and MQSPR. Specif-
ically, we prove that UMQ and MQSPR are equivalent, that MQOW implies
UMQ, and that UMQ implies MQOW under some condition. These results iden-
tify MQOW as a foundational assumption underlying both UMQ and MQSPR
in multivariate cryptography.
